summary: Canadian Coast Guard light on Bliss Island in the Bay of Fundy, first lit 1 December 1871. The red flash now shows from a skeleton tower beside a 1964 concrete tower.

structures.note: Square wooden tower, painted white (LighthouseFriends; Chance Heritage Trust). Raised in 1903 (height from base to vane given as 40 feet, about 12 m) with an octagonal iron lantern. LighthouseFriends and Rowlett put the concrete tower in its place in 1964. The sources do not say what became of the wooden tower.
Concrete tower with lantern and gallery, inactive since 2016 (Rowlett). Rowlett gives 12 m (38 ft).
One-storey concrete fog-alarm building with a square tower rising from one corner (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett).
Square skeleton tower with red and white rectangular daymark, carrying the active red light (Coast Guard list). Rowlett gives 7.5 m (25 ft).

access.note: Reached only by boat. Grounds open, tower closed (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett; Chance Heritage Trust).

events.note: Square wooden tower constructed in 1871 (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett).
Lit 1 December 1871 with a fixed red light from five flat-wick lamps (LighthouseFriends; Chance Heritage Trust). The LighthouseFriends roster begins the keeper in 1872.
A signal gun, said by LighthouseFriends to have come from Point Lepreau, fired in fog, and a fog trumpet sounded for steamers.

Fixed red changed to fixed white. The Department's report for the year ended 30 June 1901 says the change 'will be changed on January 15, 1902' (a planned date in the future tense, not a record of the change). LighthouseFriends and the Chance Heritage Trust give January 1901. Disagreement recorded in resolved_conflicts.
Fifth-order dioptric lens: occulting white, 10 s light and 5 s eclipse. Work cost $1,248.43 (Department report; the Chance Heritage Trust names Chance Brothers as lens maker).
Tower raised; the Department gives the height from base to vane as 40 feet (about 12 m). Wooden lantern replaced by an octagonal iron lantern.
Masts of the schooner Centenial, a menace to navigation, removed at Bliss Island by C.G.S. Laurentian (report for the fiscal year 1923-24).
One-storey concrete fog-alarm building with a concrete tower (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett gives 12 m).
The 1964 concrete tower inactive since 2016 (Rowlett). The active red light moved to a skeleton tower beside it (Rowlett; Coast Guard list).

corrections.proposed: deactivated 2016 applies to the 1964 concrete tower only; the active red light continues on a skeleton tower beside it
corrections.why: Rowlett says the historic lighthouse has been inactive since 2016 and the active light is on a skeleton tower next to it. The Coast Guard list still gives the active red light, year round. The record's 'deactivated' should not read as the station going dark.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: OpenStreetMap and the Coast Guard list give the station as active. Rowlett gives 'inactive since 2016'. Rowlett's note refers to the 1964 concrete tower. The active red light is on the skeleton tower beside it. The record keeps 'active'.

LighthouseFriends and the Chance Heritage Trust date the change from fixed red to fixed white to January 1901. The Department's 1901 report (year ended 30 June 1901, printed 1902) says the change 'will be changed on January 15, 1902'. The report says 'will be changed', a plan in the future tense, so it does not confirm that the change happened on that date. The story gives the report's date as a plan and notes the other two.

The Chance Heritage Trust suspects the wooden tower was replaced by concrete in 1903, but says it could not confirm the date. LighthouseFriends and Rowlett date the concrete building to 1964. The research uses 1964.

notes_for_editor: Sources: LighthouseFriends (copyrighted; paraphrased, with one short quotation from the 1872 letter it prints); Chance Heritage Trust lighthouse record; Coast Guard List of Lights (entry 77, page dated 2026-09-24); Rowlett; and Department of Marine reports in the local corpus for 1900, 1901, 1903 and 1923-24. The corpus starts in 1900, so the 1871 to 1899 history (construction, the early keepers, the 1872 fog signal, the 1873 to 1876 works) rests on LighthouseFriends alone. LighthouseFriends cites the Department's annual reports, but I did not read those reports for 1871 to 1899. Keeper McLeod (1900 to 1919): the 1900 keeper table lists a McLeod, J. H. and the station Bliss Island in separate OCR columns, so that match is by position (checked on the page image, scan p. 225, printed p. 128: the McLeod, J. H. line sits level with Bliss Island, appointed October 17, 1900; still a position match). The 1904 keeper table (scan p. 172 of 1905v39i9p21_0266) shows a similar position match, not cited. Mrs. Ester McLeod, A. Henderson, F. K. Spinney and Frederick Frye appear only in LighthouseFriends' roster; Frye has no start year. Clarke's start is 1871 in LighthouseFriends' narrative and 1872 in its roster. The colour-change date is unresolved: January 15, 1901 (LighthouseFriends, Chance Heritage Trust) against January 15, 1902 (Department report published 1902). The 1902 report (corpus volume 1903v37i8p21_0139, year ended 30 June 1902) was searched for 'Bliss' and 'fixed white' in the corpus page index: only the keeper list mentions Bliss Island (scan p. 241); no change entry was found; OCR may hide one. The 1901 report's improvements section is confirmed on the page image: the Bliss island entry is on printed p. 63 (scan p. 78), and the index gives p. 63 for it. The same report also has an earlier, undated Bliss entry on printed p. 38, a Bay of Fundy narrative saying the light 'will be greatly improved by changing it in colour from red to white'; not cited. The Wikipedia Bliss Islands article lists wrecks in 1873 (G. F. Baird), 1874 (Levi Hart) and 1881 (Nota Bene) off the islands and names Jarvis Clark as keeper in 1879. I could not trace its references from the text available, so those wrecks are not used. The Chronicling America searches for 'Bliss Island' with 'lighthouse' or 'light' (1871 to 1925) returned mostly unrelated pages, and no page was used. Current lens status and whether the 1903 lens survives are not in any source read. The skeleton tower's date is not given. Living people: none beyond the roster names, which are given only as LighthouseFriends prints them, with no personal details. Photographs: LighthouseFriends photographs are copyright (Kraig Anderson) and were not used; none with a clear licence was found. Not checked: the Canadian Coast Guard's own station pages; the 1872 to 1899 Department reports.
